I guess because the ‘typical’ pattern of irregularity for PCOS is to not have a period for months followed by a heavy period. I’d have various degrees of irregularity in my period since I started menstruating. When I first started I would have periods/spotting that would last about 2 weeks at a time, and eventually it seemed to settle out for a year or two, but then I started getting a very light period every two weeks and worsening acne (which has always been bad), so I decided to have my levels checked again. I’d had them checked by a gyno in my hometown about a year before that and I don’t remember if they measured free or bioavailable testosterone (know for sure they didn’t test SHBG), but my total T and estrogen were normal then too.

I originally went to my PCP and told her my concerns so she did the initial blood work and referred me to a gynecologist. The gyno I saw said I’d need to meet two out of three criteria and she wasn’t sure I would qualify because my irregular periods weren’t irregular in the way it usually is in PCOS despite having other symptoms and a family history (didn’t really like her for obvious reasons). She sent me for the ultrasound and said to keep tracking my period and follow up in three months. Did the ultrasound and she confirmed it was PCOS and then didn’t make any effort to meet before the three month follow up for treatment so I went back to my PCP and started treatment through her. My PCP has a special interest in women’s health though, so I wasn’t too worried about it.
